segments.t: Andrea visits the estate of star client Jean Dujardin after his family raises urgent concerns. Still deeply immersed in his wilderness movie role, Jean is camping outside in the woods and refusing all modern comforts. Let's listen to their conversation in French first.

Let's explore the conversation line by line and unpack the French phrases.
Jean? Tu es là?
'Jean? Are you there?' Andrea calls out into the dense garden foliage. The brief question 'you' checks for physical presence.
Hein? Eh, Andréa!
'Huh? Hey, Andrea!' Jean emerges abruptly from the undergrowth. The colloquial interjection 'huh' indicates sudden surprise.
Il ne fallait pas te déplacer.
'You should not have traveled out here.' Jean minimizes the necessity of her visit. The imperfect 'was necessary' frames an unnecessary effort.
Mais il y a une vraie urgence pour toi!
'But there is a real emergency for you!' Andrea highlights the critical situation. The noun phrase 'a' signals immediate crisis.
Tu as besoin d'une douche immédiatement.
'You need a shower immediately.' Andrea points bluntly to his neglected hygiene. The idiom 'have' expresses pressing personal necessity.
Oui, c'est ce que me dit ma femme aussi.
'Yes, that is what my wife tells me too.' Jean concedes his family's complaints. The relative clause 'ce que me dit' reports third-party opinions.
Ne t'inquiète pas, ce n'est pas grave.
'Do not worry, it is not serious.' Jean brushes aside her sanitary concerns. The negative phrase 'c'est pas grave' downplays the issue.
C'est l'odeur naturelle de la terre.
'It is the natural smell of the earth.' Jean romanticizes his outdoor grime. The noun 'smell' refers to sensory atmospheric scent.
Non, c'est plutôt une odeur de putréfaction.
'No, it is rather a smell of putrefaction.' Andrea counters with brutal honesty. The visceral noun 'putrefaction' describes organic decay.
Vous vivez dans un monde tellement aseptisé!
'You live in such a sanitized world!' Jean criticizes artificial modern comfort. The past participle 'sanitized' describes an excessively clean environment.
Regarde là-haut, c'est une buse.
'Look up there, that is a buzzard.' Jean spots a bird of prey overhead. The feminine noun 'buzzard' denotes a wild predatory hawk.
Tu vois comme elle tourne en rond?
'Do you see how it circles around?' Jean interprets the raptor's flight path. The phrase 'tourne en rond' describes circular hovering.
Elle vient pour me voler quelque chose.
'It is coming to steal something from me.' Jean projects paranoia onto the bird. The motion structure 'comes' expresses intended action.
Jean, tu as un rendez-vous important demain.
'Jean, you have an important meeting tomorrow.' Andrea tries to anchor him in reality. The noun phrase 'rendez-vous important' reminds him of work duties.
Ici, je me sens libre et vivant.
'Here, I feel free and alive.' Jean defends his primitive outdoor lifestyle. The adjective pair 'free' celebrates emotional liberation.
Tu dois redevenir un acteur maintenant.

'You must become an actor again now.' Andrea delivers her firm managerial verdict. The modal verb 'must' demands a return to civilized professional life. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more to lock in what you have learned.
